CITY COUNCIL

  AUGUST 8, 2022
  CLOSED SESSION: 4:00 P.M.
  PASADENA CITY HALL, COUNCIL CHAMBER
  100 NORTH GARFIELD AVENUE, ROOM S249

  NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN that a closed session special meeting of the City Council
will be held on Monday, August 8, 2022, at 4:00 p.m. This virtual meeting will be held solely
by video conference/teleconference, to discuss the following:

A.  CITY COUNCIL CONFERENCE WITH LEGAL COUNSEL regarding pending
  litigation pursuant to Government Code Section 54956.9(d)(1)
  Name of Case: Madden v. Rose Bowl Operating Company
  Los Angeles Superior Court Case No. 20STCV13061

B.  CITY COUNCIL CONFERENCE WITH LEGAL COUNSEL regarding pending
  litigation pursuant to Government Code Section 54956.9(d)(1)
  Name of Case: Vahabi and Izadmehr v. City of Pasadena and Rose Bowl
  Operating Co.
  LASC Case No.: 19STCV27647

  ________________________
  Victor M. Gordo, Mayor
  City of Pasadena

  I HEREBY CERTIFY that this notice, in its entirety, was posted on the Internet at
www.cityofpasadena.net/councilagendas and on the Council Chamber Bulletin Board, Room
S249 and the Bulletin Board in the rotunda area, City Hall, 100 North Garfield Avenue, and a
copy was distributed to Central Library for posting this 4th day of August, 2022, at 5:30 p.m.,
and that copies hereof were faxed, emailed or delivered to each member of the City Council
and to each local newspaper of general circulation, radio or television station requesting
notice in writing, all of which recipients are identified on the distribution list set forth herein
below.
  _____________________________
  Mark Jomsky, City Clerk
 NOTE TO PUBLIC: Public comment is limited to Item A and B on this special meeting agenda,
and a maximum of 20 minutes total is allotted for the public comment portion of the agenda.
Comments will be limited to 2 minutes each, but the speaking time may be reduced to ensure
that all speakers who have submitted a speaker card prior to the start of public comment
period are able to address the City Council during the 20-minute period.

  Recommendation: It is recommended that the City Council:
  (1) Approve the establishment of a Roadside Memorial Sign
  Program within the Department of Transportation; and
  (2) Approve the draft policy to execute this Program.
  Recommendation of the Municipal Services Committee: On July
  26, 2022, the Municipal Services Committee requested that the draft
  policy be modified to allow for a Council District office to submit a
  request for a Roadside Memorial Sign when the victim is an unhoused
  individual and when the next of kin cannot be identified or located
  through the collective efforts of the City. Staff has modified the policy
  to include such language. In addition, the Municipal Services
  Committee recommended that staff review if additional language
  could be included on the memorial sign, such as "In Loving Memory"
  or the addition of the date of birth and date of death of the victim. Staff
  will review this request to ensure consistency with the California
  Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices and best practices. In
  anticipation of such accommodations being allowed, the policy has
  been modified to allow for the potential for additional language on the
  sign.
  Recommendation of the Transportation Advisory Commission:

  recommended that the City Council approve the recommended staff
  policy for establishment of the Roadside Memorial Sign Program. The

I

  costs, after the useful life of the initial installation, be borne by the
  City. Staff concurs with this recommendation and has included it in
  the draft policy.

  Interim City Manager Kurtz and David Reyes, Acting Assistance City
  Manager, provided introductory comments; and responded to
  questions.

  Jay Trevino and Andrea Miller, representing Management Partners,
  presented a PowerPoint presentation on the item; and all responded
  to questions.

  Councilmember Madison raised several questions on the policy
  rational for imposing the annual fee on landlords; expressed concerns
  with potential financial effects this measure will have on landlords as
  a result of the rent control regulations, and potential for a decrease of
  property value and housing supply in the City; noting that based on
  his research, a large percentage of economist oppose rent control.

I
  Councilmember Williams echoed Councilmember Madison concerns
  regarding the anticipated public benefit of rent control in relation to
  the likely financial burden that will result on landlords, the need for a
  broader policy discussion on the annual fee, noting that affordable
  housing is a citywide matter and that cost should be distributed not

  Council Minutes  7  08/08/2022
   only to landlords but to educational institutions and employers. She
  stated the need for a financial analysis on historical rental increases

I
  over the past 10 years, including projected rents in comparison to
  Consumer Price Index (CPI) increases, as a way to quantify
  anticipated tenant benefits should the Charter Amendment measure
  be adopted. She also suggested the need for a comparison of the
  state's rent control vs the City's proposed Charter Amendment; spoke
  on the need to preserve the City's old housing market for those
  families that will benefit from rent regulated units, touching upon
  illegal subletting and finding a way to tie rent to income, and
  encouraged the City to explore opportunities to work with the
  California Statewide Community Development Authority (CSCD).

  Vice Mayor Wilson spoke on the Tenant Protection Act (AB 1482),
  which became law on January 1, 2022, and cautioned that AB 1482
  was implemented in the middle of a pandemic; expressed concern
  with potential impacts to property values and property tax revenue,
  noting that property tax is the General Fund's largest revenue source,
  which may result in potential fiscal impacts to the City.

  Following discussion, on the order of the Mayor, and consensus of
  the City Council, the information was received and filed.

  Mark Jomsky, City Clerk, reported on the correspondence received

I
  for Items 11, 12 and 13, as follows: ten letters advocating for the City
  Council to support the rent control initiative; thirty seven letters in
  opposition to the rent control ballot measure, advocating for the City
  Council to oppose the rent control measures and/or expressing
  concerns with the rent control initiative; one letter advocating for the
  City Council to be neutral or support the rent control initiative; and
  one letter advocating for changes to the proposed text of the Charter
  Amendment Rent Control Measure ballot question to include a
  clarification that rent increases are tied to the year-over-year increase
  in CPI, rent control exempts single family homes, and enumerate
  specific examples of the just cause for eviction criteria; which were
  received by the City Clerk's Office, distributed to the City Council,
  posted on-line, and made part of the public record.

   Councilmember Rivas expressed thanks and appreciation to the
  public speakers for their comments; spoke on the analysis presented,

I
  stating that there is not enough information on the resulting impacts
  of the proposed voter initiative if the measure passes; and spoke in
  support for the City Council taking a neutral position on the Charter
  Amendment Rent Control Measure, and allowing the measure to
  stand or fail on its own merits.

  Councilmember Madison and Councilmember Masuda spoke on the
  complexities surrounding the matter; expressed concerns with
  potential impacts to the landlords, while acknowledging the
  affordability concerns of tenants; and stated their support for the City
  Council to take a neutral position on the measure.

  Councilmember Williams expressed concerns with the findings of the
  report regarding the potential impacts and implementation of the
  Charter Amendment, which is not a perfect overlay with existing
  provisions of the Charter, and stated her support for the City Council
  to take a neutral position.

  Vice Mayor Wilson stated that if the measure passes, it is his hope
  that it will provide the intended positive benefits, and the negative
  implications to the landlords, housing stock and housing quality will
  not come to pass.
